item.title: Windows hides its fastest power plan from most PCs, and unlocking it takes one line
item.itunes:title: Windows hides its fastest power plan from most PCs, and unlocking it takes one line
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Windows 11 comes with plenty of features to manage power consumption and performance, but it's easy to forget that some things have been removed or hidden over time. For example, you used to change these power settings in Control Panel, and you still have that option, but Microsoft expects you to use the new Settings app, and the settings in these pages aren't exactly the same.

But there's one option that's even more hidden than the old Control Panel settings. It's the Ultimate Performance power plan, and while it's hidden on Windows 11, it's still possible to use it with a very simple tweak.

What does the Ultimate Performance power plan do?

Crank everything to the max

As you can probably guess from its name, the Ultimate Performance power plan aims to maximize your PC's performance at the expense of everything else. That includes power consumption and noise, meaning your PC may run louder and hotter than usual.

In practical terms, this power plan makes it so that your CPU is always running at max speed, rather than adjusting to your usage. In a typical scenario, your CPU will slow down when it's not doing anything demanding, and speed up when needed, but the short transition period between one mode and the other can result in tiny performance hiccups, which can be noticeable depending on your use case.

Likewise, a mechanical hard drive may constantly be spinning so that latency in file access is reduced, your USB devices may be prevented from going to sleep, and a few other things. It's all about ensuring that every part of your setup is always ready to go full bore to give you the best performance possible.

I make this one change to make Windows faster

One simple toggle can speed up your Windows experience

15
By  Ty Sherback

This power plan is mostly aimed at desktop workstations, and enabling it on a laptop is something I would strongly advise against. However, if you need unwavering performance all the time, this is the plan for you.

How to enable the Ultimate Performance plan

It's fairly easy

The Ultimate Performance power plan may be hidden, but you can enable it with a single PowerShell command. Simply open Windows Terminal on your PC and enter this command:

powercfg -duplicatescheme e9a42b02-d5df-448d-aa00-03f14749eb61Once you've done this, you can open Control Panel, switch the view to Small icons (or Large icons) and then choose Power Options. The Ultimate Performance plan should be there now.

However, there's a major caveat to this. As mentioned above, the plan is aimed squarely at desktop users needing the absolute best performance. I've attempted to enable this plan on two laptops and a mini PC (which also uses a laptop-grade CPU), and in all cases, the Ultimate Performance plan didn't appear. In fact, only the Balanced plan is available.

4 tweaks I always make to get more performance from my Windows 11 gaming handheld

I aim to strike a balance between how good a game looks and its frame rate.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

When testing on a desktop, however — or even in a virtual machine running inside a laptop — the command works without issues, so you can go ahead and enable it. It shouldn't require a reboot, so if you don't see any changes after running the command, it likely means your PC simply won't support it.

While we strongly advise against, if you absolutely must access this power plan (or others hidden on Windows 11 laptops), this YouTube video includes a link to a file you can use to forcefully restore the missing power plans. I tested it and it does achieve that goal without any apparent malware on board, but it's always good to be cautious. Especially considering that, even if it works, it likely won't benefit you.

Should you actually use it?

Probably not

Enabling the Ultimate Performance power plan is easy enough, but is there a good enough reason to actually do it? Even if you have a desktop where the power plan makes some sense, you're probably better off without it.

The benefits of running things like your CPU and HDD at max speed all the time are negligible in almost all situations. Very few workloads and people need that kind of constant performance and responsiveness, and the period it takes for a processor or disk to ramp up when needed is very short. You'd almost never see a difference.

At the same time, there are some real downsides to running your PC like this. Your CPU will run hotter and you might need to upgrade your thermal paste sooner, or you might end up killing your CPU altogether. The same can go for your hard drive; keeping your disk spinning all the time is going to create a higher risk of a mechanical failure happening sooner rather than later, which is obviously a big risk.

I disabled these 7 background services to boost Windows performance

These are services I can safely disable to make Windows more responsive.

5
By  Brian Burgess

That's not even addressing laptops, where you will almost certainly destroy your device's battery much quicker than necessary. Unless you're planning to stay plugged in all the time and bypassing the battery altogether, not only will the battery die faster each time, but the total capacity will be reduced more quickly.

Still, for very specific use cases, it has its place, and that's why the feature exists in the first place. Remember, this isn't some ancient feature that's still kept around by chance, it was introduced in Windows 10 just eight years ago.

It's hidden for a reason

It's easy to understand why the Ultimate Performance power plan isn't immediately available to Windows users. After all, the risk is too high for the reward in the vast majority of cases, though it would be nice to have this more readily available on any machine, even if it remains hidden. Still, if you need it, following the steps above is all you need.

item.title: I went hands-on with XREAL’s Android XR glasses, and I didn’t want to take them off
item.itunes:title: I went hands-on with XREAL’s Android XR glasses, and I didn’t want to take them off
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Like everyone else following the XR space, I’ve been reading about Android XR and Google’s plans for the platform for quite a while now. Ironically, I even wrote about XREAL’s Project Aura when the company first announced the glasses alongside Google at I/O last year.

At the time, I understood what Google and XREAL were trying to build on paper. However, it wasn’t until I finally got to put the glasses on myself that I really got it. And, well, I didn’t want to take them off.

XREAL Aura is getting very close to launch

The finish line is in sight

At Google I/O 2026, Google and XREAL first announced Project Aura, which was described as a pair of lightweight, tethered XR glasses built on Android XR,. At that time, though, there wasn't really much to go on beyond the basic idea. XREAL showed off the hardware, confirmed that Gemini would be built with, and promised a much wider field of view than its existing glasses. Of course, a lot has changed since then. Project Aura has since become XREAL Aura, and the glasses are officially expected to launch this fall.

So while media certainly got to try Project Aura earlier this year at Google I/O 2026, the version I got my hands on at IFA comes at a very different point in the product's journey. Aura is now just months away from launch, reservations are already open, and XREAL has revealed considerably more about what the final experience is supposed to look like.

That doesn't necessarily mean the unit I tried was final hardware or software, and there were definitely a few reminders during my demo that Aura isn't quite ready to ship just yet. But for the first time, I got to experience what XREAL and Google have been promising for myself — and it took me very little time to understand why they're so excited about it.

It’s like the Vision Pro and Meta’s smart glasses had a baby

The best of both worlds

The easiest way I can describe XREAL Aura is that it feels like the Apple Vision Pro and a pair of Meta smart glasses had a baby. You get the sort of spatial computing experience I'd normally associate with a full-blown headset (floating windows, hand tracking, apps anchored around you, and all) but packed into something that looks and feels much closer to a pair of glasses.

On paper, there's quite a bit going on here, too. Aura weighs under 95 grams and uses micro-OLED displays with a 70-degree field of view and a 120Hz refresh rate. There are also two SLAM sensors for depth and spatial tracking, along with a 12MP camera. Most of the heavy lifting is handled by the Snapdragon Reality Elite chip inside the 270-gram puck, while XREAL's own X1S chip sits inside the glasses and handles some of the spatial processing and display control. XREAL says that combination helps keep latency under 3ms, which definitely became noticeable once I actually started moving windows around.

Of course, running Android XR entirely on a pair of glasses this light would be a pretty tall order, which is where that puck comes in. It's tethered to the Aura and handles most of the heavy lifting, essentially letting XREAL keep the glasses themselves relatively lightweight without stripping away the kind of spatial computing experience you'd normally expect from a much bulkier headset.

On the glasses, you'll find a few physical controls as well. Pressing and holding the button on the upper-left side brings up Gemini, while the red button underneath lets you adjust the lens dimming. Holding that same button down clears up your workspace by tidying away the windows around you (similar to cleaning up a cluttered desktop on a Mac). There's also a simple volume rocker, so most of the basic controls are still within easy reach without having to rely entirely on gestures.

Comfort-wise, I was pleasantly surprised. My demo lasted close to 40 minutes, and I never found Aura uncomfortable to wear during that time. XREAL also supports prescription lens inserts, which is an important practical touch for anyone who normally wears glasses.

Using Android XR felt surprisingly natural

Point, pinch, done

If you aren't all that familiar with what Android XR feels and looks like in practice, the easiest way to think about it is Android reworked for a spatial interface. Instead of everything living on a single screen, apps can sit in floating windows around you, and you interact with them using hand gestures rather than taps and swipes.

My demo began with learning a few of the basic hand gestures, and as someone who isn't exactly the greatest at picking up new gesture controls, it did take me a little while to adjust. But once I got the hang of them, everything started feeling surprisingly smooth. Within a few minutes, I was pinching to select things, dragging windows around, and moving through Android XR without really having to think too hard about what my hands were doing.

XREAL walked me through a few different use cases, but Google Maps was personally my favorite. I've spent hours exploring random cities through Google Maps Street View on my 13-inch laptop. Now, imagine that same experience, except the city is blown up around you and you can look around it almost like you're actually there.

I could zoom in and out, tilt my view, and move around different parts of the map using simple hand gestures. What's interesting about Aura is that you can still technically see your surroundings the entire time, since the glasses use an optical see-through display. If you want a little more immersion, though, you can darken the lenses using the dimming control and make the virtual content stand out much more against the real world.

I tried Gemini Omni, and it's so good it feels straight out of science fiction

There's a new king of video generation in town, and it's no joke

3
By  Abhinav Raj

XREAL also walked me through a few interactive games, including one where I was surrounded by planets and had to use my hands to sling objects toward them. It was a simple demo, but it did a great job of showing off the spatial side of Android XR. Rather than interacting with something on a flat screen in front of me, I was physically looking around, reaching into the space around me, and using my hands to interact with objects that felt like they were actually sitting there.

There was another experience that let me draw freely in the space around me, with the drawing later producing a tune when I touched it. What made it especially fun was that the drawing wasn't confined to a flat canvas in front of me. I could actually walk around the entire thing I had just created, look at it from different angles, and interact with different parts of it as if it were physically sitting in the room with me.

All of it just felt extremely futuristic, and in the grand scheme of things, these were fairly simple demos. However. that was almost what made them so impressive.

Gemini is where Aura gets really interesting

Context really is king

Think about it. AI becomes infinitely more useful when it has all the context. That's precisely why practically every prompt-engineering guide tells you to front-load context, and why "context is king" has become such a common phrase in the AI world. Now, if the LLM at hand can see exactly what you're seeing, a huge chunk of that work is already done for you.

You don't have to explain what app you're in, what you're trying to do, or what's currently sitting in front of you. Gemini already has that visual context, which means you can simply ask the question you'd naturally ask another person standing beside you and have it respond based on what you're actually looking at.

With the XREAL Aura, you can also plug it into your laptop and use the glasses as a spatial display. That becomes especially interesting once Gemini is thrown into the mix, because it can understand what you're looking at on that screen and help you based on the context already in front of you. So, instead of taking a screenshot of something you're stuck on, uploading it to an AI assistant, and explaining what you're trying to do, you can simply ask Gemini while you're still looking at it. For instance, I plugged in my Mac, opened Canva, and asked Gemini how I'd resize a window. Gemini then guided me based on the interface I was already looking at.

The experience, as a whole, reminded me a lot of this tool called Clicky that I wrote about on XDA. Clicky can see what's happening on your screen and guide you through whatever you're doing in real time, without forcing you to constantly stop and explain the context.

Gemini on Aura felt like a much more immersive version of that same idea, except instead of living beside your cursor, it can understand what you're looking at through the glasses and help you right there.

XREAL Aura is coming this fall for no more than $1,500

While XREAL hasn't announced exact pricing for Aura just yet, the company has confirmed that the base model will cost no more than $1,500 before tax. Reservations are already open, with a $199 refundable priority deposit that goes toward the final purchase price. Aura is currently expected to launch in the US, UK, Korea, and Japan this fall, with Europe following shortly after.

If I were writing this article before having experienced XREAL Aura, this paragraph might have been focused on how difficult it is to justify spending up to $1,500 on a pair of glasses. And don't get me wrong, that's still a lot of money. But after actually using Aura, I understand the price a lot more than I expected to. The Vision Pro starts at $3699, and while the XREAL Aura glasses certainly don't compare to them in every way, it's still trying to deliver a lot of the same spatial-computing appeal into something that's considerably lighter and closer to an actual pair of glasses!

Ultimately, my short demo was enough to leave me wanting considerably more time with it. For once, giving the glasses back was easily the worst part of the demo!

item.title: Apple's new iPhone 18 Pro features a variable aperture and a huge battery life upgrade
item.itunes:title: Apple's new iPhone 18 Pro features a variable aperture and a huge battery life upgrade
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
At Apple's annual fall hardware keynote, the tech giant showcased the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, the latest versions of its flagship smartphone.

The new phone is available in Deep Black, Silver, Glacier, and Burgundy, along with color-matched rear glass. Both phones also feature Apple's new A20 Pro chip built on 2nm technology, which the tech giant says is highly power-efficient and offers the biggest battery increase ever for an iPhone.

Apple says that the A20 Pro features a 6 core CPU with "desktop-class" super cores and 4 efficiency cores. Its GPU features a 7 core design with a "40 percent" jump in performance. Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro features a "next-generation vapor chamber," so in theory, it should run cooler than the iPhone 17 Pro under heavy load. The Dynamic Island is smaller now, too, and can show three different Live Activities.

The iPhone 18 Pro features several DSLR-like photography features

The new variable aperture aims to give you more control over your photos

Credit: Apple

On the camera front, there's a lot to unpack. The phone features a 48-megapixel main camera with a variable aperture that works a lot like like a DSLR. In dark environments, you can open up the aperture to allow in more light. This gives users more control over depth-of-field and blur, and improves the performance of shooting photos at night.

Both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max share designs very similar to 2025's iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max, including the aluminum body and a sprawling camera bar Apple calls the "plateau." With this in mind, if you were hoping this year's iPhone 18 Pro would feature a notable visual refresh, this likely isn't the device for you.

Credit: Apple

This is Apple's first event to be helmed by the tech giant's new CEO John Ternus, who replaced Tim Cook on September 1st. The iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro are available to pre-order on Friday, September 11th, and release on September 18th. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,200, a $100 increase over the iPhone 17 Pro, while the iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,300.

During its keynote, Apple revealed its $129 AirPods 5 with improved ANC, more "natural" sounding Transparency Mode, and better durability. Additionally, Apple showed off the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, alongside a new Health Sensing system

More to come...

item.title: My speed tests were perfect, but my connection still felt awful, and one queueing setting explained it all
item.itunes:title: My speed tests were perfect, but my connection still felt awful, and one queueing setting explained it all
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
There are plenty of guides about optimizing your Wi-Fi performance. I had tried almost everything on mine, including changing the DNS servers and reducing the router's transmit power. Still, my connection hit a wall now and then, seemingly for no reason. Wi-Fi wasn't the only thing suffering; even the Ethernet connection on my PC didn't quite feel rock-solid.

That's when I checked my connection for bufferbloat, and figured out that the setting I should have changed all along was SQM, or Smart Queue Management. This feature prevents your router's packet buffer from being backed up, which can create latency in games, video calls, and even regular browsing.

4 router settings most people never change that actually fix slow Wi-Fi

Don't blame your router or internet plan before checking your router's settings

3
By  Tanveer Singh

I couldn't pinpoint why my connection just gave up sometimes

I had admitted defeat

My 200 Mbps plan has been more than enough for my use case. I don't have too many devices in the house; it's just my PC, an iMac, two phones, two laptops, and a smart TV. There are no home automation devices dragging the Wi-Fi down either. On top of that, I switch the wireless channel every now and then based on a fresh scan, and even enabled basic QoS on the router.

While the Wi-Fi connection remained stable and fast enough most of the time, there were instances where it mysteriously slowed down. My Instagram feed started buffering, YouTube on TV wasn't responsive enough, and even my WhatsApp uploads took longer than usual. Wi-Fi is one thing, but even my PC's wired connection felt subpar sometimes. The download speeds were fine, but webpages took slightly longer to load.

This is the kind of infrequent behavior that's hard to explain or pinpoint to a specific culprit. I assumed it was just one of those unsolvable internet issues until I realized I hadn't checked for bufferbloat.

Your neighbors' Wi-Fi is slowing yours down, and one simple setting can fix it

Your router's default wireless channel may not be the most optimal

4
By  Tanveer Singh

SQM was the setting I had been ignoring all along

It had the biggest impact on my connection

Smart Queue Management (SQM) was something I didn't think I needed. After all, I was rarely pushing even my 200 Mbps connection to its limits. However, the few instances when my connection slowed down could be linked to the times when a heavy download or 4K stream was hogging all the bandwidth. The router's buffer or queue was filled up, and any additional packets were being held in the buffer, creating a perceptible lag.

This phenomenon is called bufferbloat, where your router doesn't drop data packets, but leads to high latency, despite speed tests showing everything is normal. QoS can help prioritize traffic, but SQM is what truly attacks bufferbloat, breaking up a single packet queue into smaller sub-queues for every data stream. It automatically detects time-sensitive traffic from online games, video calls, or webpage requests, pushing them to the front of the queue.

You can find SQM under the advanced network settings on your router's admin page. To enable it, you'll need to enter your actual download and upload speeds. These should be 85–90% of the tested numbers, so that your router becomes the traffic manager instead of depending on the router-ISP link. Your maximum bandwidth will be reduced, but the latency benefits that you'll experience will be worth it.

Once I had activated the setting on my router, I started seeing the impact on both my Wi-Fi and Ethernet performance. 4K streams started buffering less, doomscrolling became snappier, and my internet felt more responsive overall. If your ISP router doesn't expose SQM, you'll need an aftermarket router with firmware that supports CAKE or FQ-CoDEL algorithms needed for true SQM.

Your guest network is probably faster than your main network, and it's because you optimized it to death

The reason embarrassed me.

1
By  Jasmine Mannan

Bufferbloat silently makes your connection sluggish

The problem with bufferbloat is that you can't easily detect it. It doesn't show up frequently, and even when it does, you often attribute the impact to something else. Fixing it with SQM in the router's settings was something I got around to quite late in the diagnosis stage, after I had tried almost everything else. If you're facing unexplained slowdown on your network, start with SQM if you've ticked the basics already.

item.title: I ditched Ollama for Jan after realizing what I actually wanted from local AI
item.itunes:title: I ditched Ollama for Jan after realizing what I actually wanted from local AI
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've used enough local LLM tools to know that self-hosting one isn't particularly difficult anymore. Ollama made that pretty obvious to me, and even learning how to use llama.cpp through the command line took only a day to learn properly. item.title: I lost my entire Jellyfin server to a dead drive, but my real mistake was the backup I thought I had
item.itunes:title: I lost my entire Jellyfin server to a dead drive, but my real mistake was the backup I thought I had
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Ever since I offloaded my Jellyfin server from my desktop PC to an old laptop, I've thought of it as something I'd never have to bother with as it ran in the background forever. The files are there, Jellyfin works smoothly, and I even have a backup. Plus, the laptop itself serves as a UPS with its battery, meaning it will keep running in the event of a power outage, so nothing much could go wrong.

Turns out, quite a lot can go wrong. Considering I had repurposed an old laptop and external HDD to function as my server, I wasn't completely surprised about the HDD dying, but when it did happen, I got a very quick lesson in the difference between having a backup and actually having a backup of your Jellyfin server.

Losing access to my media was just the beginning, and it wasn't even the surprising part. I happened to discover just how much of my setup lived somewhere other than the media itself. My backup could bring my files back, sure, but it couldn't necessarily bring my Jellyfin back with them. Things got pretty interesting from there on.

4 free Jellyfin tools that make my media server feel like a premium streaming service

I've caught the automation bug, I'm afraid

2
By  Samarveer Singh

I never expected to lose my Jellyfin server out of the blue

I gave a 10-year-old HDD one last job

The hard drive that became my Jellyfin server wasn't exactly new. I'd pulled it from a drawer after roughly 10 years of use, and it also spent the previous couple of years doing nothing. It still worked, though, and pairing it with an old laptop seemed like a better fate than leaving both of those things to gather dust.

I'd initially kept my server on my desktop PC, but decided to offload it to an old laptop connected to an even older external HDD. The laptop ran Jellyfin, and the resurrected external HDD held my movies and TV shows — pretty simple on the face of it. I wasn't building a NAS or some sort of enterprise server, either; this was just a spare laptop and an old drive doing something useful.

Restoring my media files wasn't the same as restoring Jellyfin, and that was the distinction I'd overlooked.

Then, the HDD stopped responding out of the blue, with no warning or countdown. One moment Jellyfin was serving my library, and the next, it couldn't find the files. Plugging the HDD into my PC showed me the problem — it was no longer recognized, and no amount of troubleshooting brought it back. One fine day, my oldest HDD died, and took all my movies, TV shows, and home videos with it.

Thankfully, I wasn't fretting, since my backup strategy involved a second copy of all my media. The movies and shows weren't gone forever, but restoring those files wasn't the same as restoring Jellyfin — it was that distinction that turned out to be the part of my backup strategy I'd overlooked.

I'm buying an 8TB external HDD instead of an 8TB external SSD, and the price is just one reason why

It's all about the performance, reliability, and convenience of an external HDD

9
By  Tanveer Singh

My backup saved only the files, not my Jellyfin server

I had backed up what Jellyfin watched, not what it remembered

It was reassuring to see that my media wasn't gone entirely. I had a second copy of the movies and TV shows, so replacing the failed drive was merely a matter of copying everything back. For a moment, I genuinely believed I'd dodged a bullet.

Then I remembered that Jellyfin isn't just a folder browser. The server keeps data that includes configuration, library definitions, users, watch history, resume positions, metadata, and the settings for all the plugins I regularly experiment with. Sadly, none of these settings live inside the movie file itself.

Users can install Jellyfin on their PCs as a portable folder instead of a Windows service.

My backup had preserved the content, but not the experience I'd built around it. As such, I quickly reinstalled Jellyfin and got a fresh new server up and running. Sadly, this new server didn't know which episodes I'd watched, where I'd stopped, or how I'd configured the server.

This is the part I had clearly misunderstood. I was treating the media folder as though it were the server, when it was just the largest part of it. Jellyfin's data directory was carrying data I'd never thought to protect — plugins I'd spent hours configuring and playback history I always loved sifting through every month.

So my backup wasn't useless, but it certainly was incomplete. It protected the files I could rebuild Jellyfin around, but they left the server's memory behind. That's more annoying than losing a movie folder. Rebuilding media is tedious. Rebuilding watch history and settings is personal.

Everytime I set up a new Jellyfin server, these are the plugins I install first

These add-ons bring Jellyfin up to par with its premium, paid rivals

3
By  Samarveer Singh

I've learned a new Jellyfin backup strategy

Two copies, two things worth protecting

After the Jellyfin server failure, I didn't replace my cobbled-together server with a NAS or build some elaborate 3-2-1 backup system. I've still changed something, though, and I've stopped treating my media folder as the entire server. The new rule is straightforward: keep a second copy of the media, and separately back up Jellyfin's data and configuration so the server itself can be rebuilt.

The second backup now covers the stuff that I absolutely hated recreating — users, libraries, settings, watch history, resume positions, metadata, and the database. I don't have to preserve every temporary file that Jellyfin creates, though. Cache and transcoding data can be regenerated, so there's little point in wasting backup space on it. The goal is to preserve the server's state, not every byte it happens to produce.

The exact folder depends on how Jellyfin is installed. On Windows as a service, the important directory is C: > ProgramData > Jellyfin > Server. Jellyfin packages on Jellyfin use /var/lib/jellyfin for data and /etc/jellyfin/ for configuration.

If you've got a portable Windows installation, it normally uses %LOCALAPPDATA%\jellyfin.

Thankfully, it doesn't require anything fancy. My second external HDD can hold both the media backup and Jellyfin's important server data, with regular updates instead of another decade-long retirement plan. For a manual backup, I stop Jellyfin, copy those data/config folders to my backup drive, and start the server again. That's it.

Jellyfin is one of the best Plex alternatives you can get, and that's thanks to its open-source nature and powerful set of features. There are apps for basically every platform and it's completely free to run your very own server.

Jellyfin 12 will break some home servers, and I'm okay with that

Jellyfin 12 could break some home servers, but its stricter upgrade path may be exactly what the project needs to stay healthy in the long term.

2
By  Jeff Butts

My cheap hardware taught me an expensive lesson

My HDD spent years being useful, then years being forgotten before it finally found a second life as the heart of a home server, all before it decided it had done quite enough. I can't even be particularly annoyed at it. Ten years is a respectable innings for a drive, and I was the one who decided to trust it with something I cared about.

The useful part of the failure is that it exposed a mistake while the consequences were still manageable. A Jellyfin server doesn't need a complicated backup strategy to be resilient; it needs one that reflects what actually makes the server valuable. Once you understand that distinction, the backup itself becomes pretty darn boring. When it's all said and done, boring is exactly what I want from my server now.

item.title: Dell’s XPS 13 packs premium features into a budget laptop for students
item.itunes:title: Dell’s XPS 13 packs premium features into a budget laptop for students
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A college laptop has a demanding job. It needs to be light enough to carry all day, powerful enough for years of coursework, and affordable enough to meet a student budget.

Dell brought the XPS name back in 2026, and the XPS 13 combines those essentials with premium features typically found on more expensive laptops. Here’s why it could be one of the best Windows 11 laptops for students and the only computer you need from your first lecture through graduation.

Credit: Dell

It starts at $999 (CAD) for students

Dell XPS 13 (2026)
CPU
Intel Core 5 320
GPU
Intel Graphics
Display type
IPS
Display (Size, Resolution)
13.4-inch, Touch, 2.5K, 30-120Hz, 500 nits
RAM
8 GB or 16 GB of LPDDR5x
Battery
52 Wh 3-cell

The Dell XPS 13, starting at $999 (CAD) for students, is built for long days on campus, with a 2.2-pound aluminum design, all-day battery life, and a sharp 2.5K touchscreen. It has enough power for research, assignments, video calls, and entertainment, with more powerful configurations available for demanding coursework.

Ports
2x USB-C 10 Gbps with DP alt mode and PD
See at Dell

The Dell XPS 13 starts at around $999 (CAD) with an Intel® Core™ 5 320 processor from Intel’s new Wildcat Lake family, 8GB of LPDDR5X memory, and a 256GB PCIe 4.0 SSD. Student pricing even starts at $849 (CAD), making this one of the most affordable XPS laptops Dell has released in years.

Interestingly, Dell has not stripped the base model down to a low-resolution screen or minimal storage. You’ll still get the 13.4-inch 2.5K touchscreen, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0, and support for two external displays.

Premium design that won't weigh you down

Credit: Dell

Students rarely use their laptops in one place. Between lectures, group projects, library sessions, and the trip home, you need something that will not become a burden by the end of the day. The XPS 13 weighs just 2.2 lbs and measures 12.7mm thick, making it the thinnest and lightest XPS laptop Dell has ever made. It easily slips into a backpack, tote bag, or laptop sleeve without taking up much room or adding unnecessary weight.

Despite its compact dimensions, the XPS 13 still looks and feels like a premium laptop. Dell uses a CNC-machined aluminum chassis that should hold up better to the knocks and scrapes campus life brings than the plastic construction commonly found at this price. Its minimalist design also looks just as appropriate in a lecture hall as it does during an internship or presentation.

The Dell XPS 13 also features a full-size backlit keyboard, another feature that is not guaranteed on laptops in this price range. The illuminated keys make it easier to keep typing in a dim lecture hall, during a late-night library session, or while finishing an assignment after your roommate has turned off the lights.

A sharp touchscreen for work and downtime

Credit: Dell

Touchscreens are still far from standard on laptops, especially at this price, but the XPS 13 has one. It gives students a more natural way to scroll through lengthy research papers, zoom in on diagrams, navigate spreadsheets, or tap through presentation slides without always reaching for the trackpad.

The display itself is a 13.4-inch InfinityEdge panel with a sharp 2.5K resolution, giving text, images, and videos more detail than a typical Full HD screen. Slim bezels help Dell fit that screen into the XPS 13’s compact chassis, while 100% DCI-P3 color coverage makes it equally suited to creative projects and winding down with a movie after class.

It should feel smooth in daily use, too. The refresh rate can climb to 120Hz when scrolling or navigating Windows, then drop as low as 30Hz when idle to save battery power. Moreover, the display has a peak brightness of 500 nits, which helps the screen remain easy to see in brightly lit classrooms and other indoor spaces.

Battery that lasts the entire school day

Finding an outlet between classes should not be part of your daily routine. The XPS 13 packs a 52Wh battery that can last up to 18 hours and 26 minutes with Wi-Fi web browsing, according to Notebookcheck. Whether attending lectures or doing research and coursework, the XPS 13 should comfortably cover a full day with power left for some binge-watching afterward.

On the connectivity front, the Dell XPS 13 includes two fast 10Gbps USB-C 3.2 Gen 2 ports with charging and DisplayPort support. An upcoming Core Ultra 7 Panther Lake configuration will upgrade those ports to 40Gbps Thunderbolt 4 for even faster file transfers. There is no headphone jack, SD card reader, or USB-A port, though, so you may need wireless headphones or a USB-C hub for older accessories.

Performance you can configure around your major

Now, the Intel® Core™ 5 320 is not built to win benchmark charts, but it has enough power to run Windows 11 smoothly and handle the work most students do every day, including browsing with multiple tabs open, writing papers, joining video calls, and working in Microsoft Office. It combines two performance cores and four low-power efficiency cores, reaching speeds of up to 4.6GHz. Its modest 15W base power also helps the XPS 13 stay quiet while using less battery during lighter tasks.

The base configuration starts with 8GB of LPDDR5X memory, but it's configurable with 16GB if you need more breathing room for multitasking. That means you’re not hard-capped to the 8GB found on most models in the same price range. That said, the memory is soldered and cannot be upgraded later.

For demanding majors, students can step up to the upcoming Core Ultra 7 Panther Lake configuration. It increases the core count to eight, adds a more capable NPU for on-device AI features, and can be paired with up to 32GB of memory and a 1TB SSD.

Brought to you by Dell.

item.title: I changed one Android Auto setting, and I don't miss the bottom taskbar at all now
item.itunes:title: I changed one Android Auto setting, and I don't miss the bottom taskbar at all now
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been an Android Auto user for years, but until recently, I had no clue you could move the in-car infotainment system's taskbar.

It's not that I hate the left-hand side app taskbar location my Kia K4 Hatchback defaults to with Android Auto; I just often find myself in the passenger seat and would prefer the app overlay at the bottom in those situations. Even when I'm not the passenger princess, I've found it easier to reach across the bottom of the screen to select Android Auto apps, since I often fumble with the crowded left-hand side menu. Then, just a few days ago, my taskbar randomly shifted back to the left-hand side, and media controls reappeared inside apps.

Suddenly, toggling Android Auto's Quick Controls on my Pixel 11 Pro no longer moved the taskbar back to the bottom of my vehicle's display. This is a massive bummer because, over the past few weeks, I've grown to really prefer the task bar and media controls appearing at the bottom of the screen.

I tried disconnecting and reconnecting my phone, clearing Android Auto's cache, and more — nothing worked. Then, thankfully, I discovered there's a simple setting that makes accessing Android Auto's newer media controls a bit less painful.

If toggling Quick Controls doesn't work anymore for you, try this alternative

You can shift your on-screen media controls to the left or right

Until recently, toggling on Quick Controls didn't just control the taskbar's location. Along with moving it to the bottom of the screen, it also worked as a home for on-screen media controls. This setup was a near-perfect blend of Android Auto's older and newer layout. When Android Auto's media controls defaulted to the bottom of the screen, you'd see interaction options like play, pause, and skip when music or a podcast is playing.

On the other hand, with the left-leaning taskbar layout I'm stuck with now, these media options appear directly inside the split-screen app box with apps like Apple Music and Pocket Casts. With this layout, though, you can actually change where these media apps appear by navigating to Settings > Change Layout > Media Closer to Driver directly in Android Auto on your car's screen. This lets you move the media controls to the right or left side of your vehicle's screen, making them a bit easier to reach and slightly less annoying.

In my case, I keep the controls on the left because they're much easier to access when I'm behind the wheel. It's not the same as Quick Controls moving the taskbar and media controls, but it's better than reaching over to the right side of the screen to stop/start music or skip tracks when I'm behind the wheel. If I'm in the passenger seat, I simply tap Navigation Closer to Driver so that the media controls are easier to reach from the right side of the car.

Before the Quick Controls setting stopped working, the taskbar automatically moved to the bottom of the screen when I toggled the feature on, giving the media controls a dedicated, consistent location that I built up muscle memory around. I found this way easier to access as both a passenger and a driver, even though the controls are relatively small. This likely has something to do with it more closely mimicking the app layout of my Pixel 11 Pro's app dock.

If your car's display is widescreen-oriented, you're likely in the same situation

Some have gotten Quick Controls to appear again by changing Android Auto's resolution

If you have a vehicle with a relatively modern screen, you're likely in the same situation as me, and toggling Quick Controls on/off no longer does anything (a recent Android Auto update seems to have removed the layout option). Some Android Auto users have solved this issue by clearing Android Auto's cache by following these steps: Settings > Apps > See All Apps > Android Auto > Storage & Cache > Clear Cache.

In other cases, reports suggest that changing Android Auto's resolution can solve the problem, though this didn't work for me. To do that, make sure Android Auto's developer mode is enabled. On my Pixel device, I did this by going to Connected Devices > Connection Preferences > Android Auto.

Next, tap Version several times until a message appears stating that Developer Settings have been enabled. Then I tapped the three dots in the top-left corner of the screen, and scrolled down to Video Resolution. Your best bet is to allow the car and phone to negotiate the display output resolution rather than selecting a specific resolution. This method didn't work for me, but you might have better luck.

If none of the above options work, you're likely stuck with the in-app split-screen media controls and left or right-leaning taskbar. It's not a perfect solution, but changing where your media apps appear with the Layout option can go a long way towards making this sudden UI change less painful.

Even if you can get the bottom taskbar working on your vehicle's display, its days are likely numbered. Google is preparing a major Android Auto visual overhaul that significantly changes how media controls and other interface elements are displayed, with the redesign expected to roll out more broadly later this year.

I've been an Android Auto user for years, but until recently, I had no clue you could move the in-car infotainment system's taskbar.

It's not that I hate the left-hand side app taskbar location my Kia K4 Hatchback defaults to with Android Auto; I just often find myself in the passenger seat and would prefer the app overlay at the bottom in those situations. Even when I'm not the passenger princess, I've found it easier to reach across the bottom of the screen to select Android Auto apps, since I often fumble with the crowded left-hand side menu. Then, just a few days ago, my taskbar randomly shifted back to the left-hand side, and media controls reappeared inside apps.

Suddenly, toggling Android Auto's Quick Controls on my Pixel 11 Pro no longer moved the taskbar back to the bottom of my vehicle's display. This is a massive bummer because, over the past few weeks, I've grown to really prefer the task bar and media controls appearing at the bottom of the screen.

I tried disconnecting and reconnecting my phone, clearing Android Auto's cache, and more — nothing worked. Then, thankfully, I discovered there's a simple setting that makes accessing Android Auto's newer media controls a bit less painful.

If toggling Quick Controls doesn't work anymore for you, try this alternative

You can shift your on-screen media controls to the left or right

Until recently, toggling on Quick Controls didn't just control the taskbar's location. Along with moving it to the bottom of the screen, it also worked as a home for on-screen media controls. This setup was a near-perfect blend of Android Auto's older and newer layout. When Android Auto's media controls defaulted to the bottom of the screen, you'd see interaction options like play, pause, and skip when music or a podcast is playing.

On the other hand, with the left-leaning taskbar layout I'm stuck with now, these media options appear directly inside the split-screen app box with apps like Apple Music and Pocket Casts. With this layout, though, you can actually change where these media apps appear by navigating to Settings > Change Layout > Media Closer to Driver directly in Android Auto on your car's screen. This lets you move the media controls to the right or left side of your vehicle's screen, making them a bit easier to reach and slightly less annoying.

In my case, I keep the controls on the left because they're much easier to access when I'm behind the wheel. It's not the same as Quick Controls moving the taskbar and media controls, but it's better than reaching over to the right side of the screen to stop/start music or skip tracks when I'm behind the wheel. If I'm in the passenger seat, I simply tap Navigation Closer to Driver so that the media controls are easier to reach from the right side of the car.

Before the Quick Controls setting stopped working, the taskbar automatically moved to the bottom of the screen when I toggled the feature on, giving the media controls a dedicated, consistent location that I built up muscle memory around. I found this way easier to access as both a passenger and a driver, even though the controls are relatively small. This likely has something to do with it more closely mimicking the app layout of my Pixel 11 Pro's app dock.

If your car's display is widescreen-oriented, you're likely in the same situation

Some have gotten Quick Controls to appear again by changing Android Auto's resolution

If you have a vehicle with a relatively modern screen, you're likely in the same situation as me, and toggling Quick Controls on/off no longer does anything (a recent Android Auto update seems to have removed the layout option). Some Android Auto users have solved this issue by clearing Android Auto's cache by following these steps: Settings > Apps > See All Apps > Android Auto > Storage & Cache > Clear Cache.

In other cases, reports suggest that changing Android Auto's resolution can solve the problem, though this didn't work for me. To do that, make sure Android Auto's developer mode is enabled. On my Pixel device, I did this by going to Connected Devices > Connection Preferences > Android Auto.

Next, tap Version several times until a message appears stating that Developer Settings have been enabled. Then I tapped the three dots in the top-left corner of the screen, and scrolled down to Video Resolution. Your best bet is to allow the car and phone to negotiate the display output resolution rather than selecting a specific resolution. This method didn't work for me, but you might have better luck.

If none of the above options work, you're likely stuck with the in-app split-screen media controls and left or right-leaning taskbar. It's not a perfect solution, but changing where your media apps appear with the Layout option can go a long way towards making this sudden UI change less painful.

Even if you can get the bottom taskbar working on your vehicle's display, its days are likely numbered. Google is preparing a major Android Auto visual overhaul that significantly changes how media controls and other interface elements are displayed, with the redesign expected to roll out more broadly later this year.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Anthropic insider warns AI could "kill all humans," with a less than 10% chance within the next decade.
  • Anthropic and OpenAI are racing toward self-improving superintelligence, "gambling with our lives."
  • Current models are low risk now, but recursive self-improvement and breaches are warning shots.

Welcome to The Terminator IRL.

According to an Anthropic safety researcher, there's a greater than 10% chance that AI could "kill all humans." This dystopian statement comes after an employee quit at Anthropic and said that AI giants are "gambling with our lives." These concerning comments come as the AI race heats up, and both Anthropic and OpenAI continue to raise massive amounts of money while barreling towards inevitable IPOs.

According to Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic who recently left the company, neither Anthropic nor OpenAI is acting responsibly in their ongoing AI development (via CNBC). In a post on Twitter, Coxon said, "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."

"Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing," wrote Coxon.

He went on to say that "people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."

Those odds aren't that bad... right?

Superintelligence could come from recursive self-improvement

This is where Evan Hubinger, an alignment science lead who still works at Anthropic, comes in with their own perspective in a recent X post. According to Hubinger, Coxon's assessment is correct, and he does "earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!" However, he also mentions that the risk from current AI models is "low." Cool, that makes me feel better.

"What I am worried about is superintelligence arising from recursive self-improvement, as we have said is happening faster than we thought," wrote Hubinger.

In a recent blog post, Anthropic outlined that "full recursive self-improvement" could result in "humans losing control over AI systems." We already have examples of this happening to some extent. For example, an OpenAI model breached Hugging Face back in July. In an X post, Coxon calls the Hugging Face incident a "warning shot."

In other AI news, Nvidia recently acquired Hugging Face for $12.93 billion. OpenAI also recently launched GPT-6 Astra and labeled it the start of its "AGI era."

Trump says he is banning all federal agencies from using Anthropic

The AI platform isn't bowing to the Pentagon.

2
By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: Every ESP32 program you've written has been ignoring half the chip
item.itunes:title: Every ESP32 program you've written has been ignoring half the chip
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most ESP32 boards have a dual-core Xtensa processor under the hood, but you've probably only used a single core in all of your projects. That's not abnormal behavior; the second core is right there, sitting idle most of the time. You're essentially using only half the silicon you paid for.

The second core is responsible for handling background activity on the board while the primary core runs your code. However, it's possible to make use of the second core if you want to. For projects that can leverage the additional processing power, it's worth considering.

Not all ESP32 boards are the same, and picking the wrong one wastes weeks of your project time

Look for the wireless capability you need, not the name on the board

By  Joe Rice-Jones

Everything just works, so you don't notice the second core

It's always working behind the scenes

The reason most people don't ever think about the second core on their ESP32 is that it remains in the background. The two Xtensa cores, labeled Core 0 and Core 1, are identical in hardware capability but different in their roles. Core 1, called the APP_CPU (Application CPU), is the one running your setup() and loop() routines in Arduino IDE, whereas Core 0, the PRO_CPU (Protocol CPU), handles the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth activity, among other things.

You can even confirm this by calling xPortGetCoreID() inside loop(), and printing the result. You'll see it report "1" for every sketch and project you run on your ESP32. Core 0 isn't exactly unused, since it's responsible for running the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth stack, but it mostly sits idle when your code runs on Core 1. The latter is well-equipped to handle most sketches and projects, so you don't feel anything is off.

Why the ESP32-S3 is the best $8 you'll ever spend on your smart home

Stop overpaying and ditch the cloud

By  Samir Makwana

But you might be missing out on more than you think

The right project can encounter a bottleneck

Running your main code on Core 1 is fine most of the time, but you're losing real power by not leveraging the second core. In projects that combine slow operations such as Bluetooth transfers, display refreshes, and network calls, which could block something that needs to run frequently, using a single core can become a bottleneck.

Suppose your code is reading an I2C sensor and streaming data over Bluetooth in the same loop. Core 1 will have to wait on one blocking operation before it can start the next one, capping the maximum performance. Everything is running serially on a single core, wasting the potential of the second one.

That said, you can bind a particular task to a specific core using the xTaskCreatePinnedToCore() function. By explicitly assigning a task to Core 0, you're ensuring effective parallel processing, making full use of your ESP32's silicon. You can keep your primary sensor reads, display updates, and control logic on Core 1, while the delay-tolerant activity like SD writes and non-blocking network calls are reserved for Core 0.

AI is right about ESP32 pins two-thirds of the time, and that's worse than always being wrong

You can use a cloud LLM to help with your microcontrollers, but it gets kind of weird with the ESP32.

By  Adam Conway

You're trading a bottleneck for some complexity

But handling it is simple enough

There's a real caveat to explicity assigning tasks to specific cores. If you bind a task to, say, Core 0 without accounting for thread-safety across cores, it can lead to a reboot if the watchdog timer detects the underlying system tasks being starved of CPU time. The fix is small yet non-negotiable.

You need to use vTaskDelay() to hand control back to the scheduler periodically, preventing the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth stack from being deprived of CPU resources. Any task you bind to Core 0 needs to yield periodically, even if the delay is just 1ms. As long as the task isn't hogging the core, it can safely co-exist with the wireless stack.

These safety mechanisms, such as mutexes and queues, are design considerations that tackle the inherent complexity of using both the cores for your project code.

Claude Code taught me ESP32 development, and my smart home projects got way faster

I didn't think I could use Claude code for this, but it worked

By  Anurag Singh

Using your ESP32's full power is possible once you know the drill

You've probably been using only the Application CPU of your ESP32 all this time, ignoring the other core completely. Well, once you know how to assign specific tasks to the Protocol CPU and put safety mechanisms in place, you can leverage all the silicon you paid for. Not every project needs both cores, so it depends on your judgment to pick the ones that can truly benefit from multi-core processing.
